paper.title: Developing and Externally Validating Machine Learning Models to Forecast Short-Term Risk of Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: To develop and externally validate supervised machine learning models using routinely collected ICU electronic health record (EHR) data to predict short-term onset of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) before clinical diagnosis.
Design: Prospective observational cohort study with temporal model development and external validation.
Setting: ICUs.
Patients: Mechanically ventilated adults in a prospective observational cohort (Successful Clinical Response In Pneumonia Therapy [SCRIPT]) who underwent bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for suspected pneumonia and had BAL-confirmed adjudicated VAP or adjudicated non-VAP status (n = 507). External validation in the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV (MIMIC-IV) included mechanically ventilated patients with greater than or equal to 48 hours of continuous invasive ventilation (n = 2681). Additional evaluation was performed in participants from the Inhaled Amikacin vs. Placebo to Prevent Ventilator Associated Pneumonia (AMIKINHAL) randomized trial evaluating inhaled amikacin for VAP prevention, using centrally adjudicated VAP outcomes.
Interventions: None.
Measurements And Main Results: We extracted 36 day-level clinical features (vital signs, ventilator settings, laboratory values, inflammatory markers, and support devices) from the EHR and trained models to predict VAP within 3, 5, or 7 days before BAL-confirmed diagnosis. Unsupervised clustering identified physiologic states enriched for VAP-labeled days. In internal testing, the best performance reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.866 for predicting VAP within 7 days and 0.843 for predicting VAP within 5 days. Predicted risk increased over the days preceding VAP among patients who developed VAP, while remaining low among non-VAP patients. On external validation in MIMIC-IV, the best model achieved an AUROC of 0.817 for predicting VAP within 5 days. Performance was poor in AMIKINHAL, where only nine of 36 features were available. Across models, influential predictors included ventilator duration and mechanics (e.g., positive end-expiratory pressure), platelet count, and inflammatory markers.
Conclusions: Machine learning models trained on day-level structured ICU data with BAL-confirmed adjudicated labels predicted VAP up to 7 days before clinical diagnosis with strong discrimination and generalized to an external health system when key features were available, supporting future prospective real-time evaluation.
authors: Northwestern University Successful Clinical Response In Pneumonia Therapy (NU SCRIPT) Study Investigators

paper.title: A Two-Stage Questionnaire for Identifying Possible Parkinson's Disease: Machine-Learning Feature Selection and Interim Prospective Validation in Almaty, Kazakhstan.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a rapidly growing cause of neurological disability, yet diagnosis is often delayed in settings with limited access to movement-disorder specialists, including Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries. This study aimed to develop a brief, self-administered, two-stage machine-learning-derived questionnaire based on binary symptom responses to identify individuals with possible clinically manifest PD who may benefit from specialist neurological assessment, and to evaluate its performance. Methods: From outpatient records of 402 patients with confirmed PD, a preliminary 100-item yes/no questionnaire was compiled. In a development cohort of 389 participants aged 60 to 90 years (146 with PD, 243 controls) recruited in Almaty, Kazakhstan, we used ElasticNet logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting to select features, reducing the instrument to 35 items (15 in Stage 1, 20 in Stage 2). We assessed performance on a held-out test set (n = 78) and in an interim prospective external-validation cohort (n = 290) recruited independently, with neurologists blinded to questionnaire results. Results: On the held-out test set, sensitivity was 86.2%, specificity 89.8%, accuracy 88.5%, and Stage 1 AUC 0.9557. In the interim external validation, sensitivity was 95.1%, specificity 94.4%, accuracy 94.5%, NPV 99.2%, and Stage 1 AUC 0.9962; only 12.1% of participants required Stage 2. Conclusions: The two-stage questionnaire showed strong case-finding ability in identifying individuals who warrant neurological evaluation. Findings are interim; completion of external validation, larger geographically diverse cohorts, and comparison against existing instruments are needed before wider implementation.

paper.title: Predicting cardiopulmonary exercise testing performance in patients undergoing transthoracic echocardiography-an artificial intelligence-based, multimodal model.
paper.abstract:
Aims: Cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) performance strongly correlates with survival in several disease states including heart failure, but has limited accessibility. Meanwhile, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is a far more widely available tool. We sought to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm using TTE and data from electronic medical records to predict CPET peak oxygen consumption (peak VO2) ≤ 14 mL/kg/min.
Methods And Results: An AI model was trained to predict peak VO2 ≤ 14 mL/kg/min from TTE images, structured TTE reports, demographics, medications, laboratory tests, and vitals. The training set included patients with a TTE within 6 months of a CPET. Performance was retrospectively tested in a held-out group from the development cohort and an external regional validation cohort. A total of 1127 CPET studies paired with concomitant TTE were identified. The best performance was achieved by using all components (TTE images, all structured clinical data). The model performed well at predicting a peak VO2 ≤ 14 mL/kg/min, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.84 (development cohort) and 0.80 (external validation cohort). It performed consistently well using higher (≤18 mL/kg/min) and lower (≤12 mL/kg/min) cut-offs.
Conclusion: This multimodal AI model effectively categorized patients into low- and high-risk predicted peak VO2, demonstrating the potential to identify previously unrecognized high-risk patients when CPET is not available.

paper.title: Machine learning-based prediction of in-hospital and post-discharge mortality in heart failure: an international retrospective study with cross-endpoint transferability analysis.
paper.abstract:
Aims: Patients with heart failure (HF) face substantial morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to build machine learning (ML) models for predicting in-hospital or post-discharge mortality in acute decompensated HF and explore whether models trained on one mortality endpoint transfer to the other.
Methods: Two retrospective HF cohorts were analyzed: 40,265 patient encounters from 15 hospitals in the United States (USA) with in-hospital mortality (3.6%) as the endpoint, and 4,892 encounters discharged alive from five hospitals in Greece (GRC) with 1-month all-cause mortality (9.2%) as the endpoint. ML models were trained using either all available features in each cohort (full models) or only variables shared between cohorts (restricted models), enabling both within-endpoint internal validation and cross-endpoint transferability assessment to be performed.
Results: During within-endpoint internal validation, discrimination was strong for the full USA models and moderate for the full GRC models, with extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) reaching an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.85 and 0.70, respectively. Advanced age and elevated admission blood urea nitrogen were the most consistent predictors. In the cross-endpoint transferability analysis, restricted XGBoost models applied to the opposite cohort retained above-chance discrimination but were significantly outperformed on the same test set by the models developed for that cohort's endpoint.
Conclusion: In two international cohorts of patients with acute decompensated HF, post-discharge mortality in the GRC cohort was more challenging to predict than in-hospital mortality in the USA cohort. XGBoost models developed for one mortality endpoint retained a degree of discriminative ability on the other endpoint, suggesting a partially shared prognostic signal between in-hospital and post-discharge mortality, while confirming the expected superiority of endpoint-specific models.

paper.title: An immunophenotype-guided interpretable subregional radiomics model for predicting local recurrence-free survival in esophageal squamous cell cancer patients treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy: a multicenter study.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: This study aimed to demonstrate tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) subtypes as prognostic factors for local recurrence-free survival (LRFS) in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) patients treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy (dCRT) and to develop an interpretable, TIME-guided subregional radiomics model for predicting LRFS.
Methods: 986 ESCC patients from three centers were enrolled. For a subset with available biopsies, multiplex immunofluorescence was used to assess CD3, CD8, and PD-L1 expression, defining prognostic TIME subtypes. Pre-treatment contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) images were used for tumor segmentation, intratumoral subregion partitioning and radiomic feature extraction. Features associated with TIME subtypes were selected to build a subregional radiomic signature (Subrad signature) for LRFS prediction using an advanced machine learning framework. This signature was integrated with clinical factors to construct a Clinic-Subregional radiomic model (CliSubrad-M).
Results: A "PD-L1-low/TILs-high" TIME subtype was identified as an independent favorable prognostic factor for LRFS (HR = 0.34, P < 0.001). The Subrad signature, comprising seven TIME-related features from various subregions, demonstrated robust predictive performance (C-indexes: 0.631-0.637). The integrated CliSubrad-M (built with Random Survival Forest) achieved the best performance, with C-indexes of 0.702 (training), 0.679 (internal testing), 0.653 (external testing1), and 0.625 (external testing2), significantly outperforming the clinical model (all P < 0.05). The model effectively stratified patients into distinct risk groups with significant differences in LRFS. SHAP analysis confirmed the signature's strong contribution and enhanced model interpretability.
Conclusions: The developed interpretable subregional radiomics model, integrating TIME biology with clinical factors, provides a non-invasive tool for predicting LRFS in ESCC received dCRT.

paper.title: PET/CT radiomics integrating tumour and whole-body composition enhances prognostic prediction in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: a multicentre study.
paper.abstract:
Purpose: To develop and validate an integrated PET/CT‑based radiomic model that combines tumour characteristics and whole‑body composition features for predicting progression‑free survival (PFS) in patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC).
Methods: This multicentre retrospective study included 477 patients with pathologically confirmed ESCC who underwent pretreatment [¹⁸F]FDG‑PET/CT. Patients were allocated to training (n = 294), internal validation (n = 74), and external validation (n = 109) cohorts. Primary tumours and whole‑body composition components, including skeletal muscle, subcutaneous adipose tissue, visceral adipose tissue, intermuscular adipose tissue and spine, were automatically segmented on PET/CT images. Radiomic features were extracted from both tumour and body‑composition regions. Feature selection and model development were performed using machine learning approaches. A composite clinical-tumour-body composition model was constructed and compared with clinical and tumour‑radiomic models.
Results: The integrated model showed superior prognostic performance over individual models, achieving C‑indices of 0.802 (95% CI: 0.770-0.832), 0.716 (95% CI: 0.639-0.797), and 0.732 (95% CI: 0.660-0.796) in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. The corresponding AUCs for 3‑year PFS prediction were 0.895 (95% CI: 0.858-0.930), 0.831 (95% CI: 0.727-0.923), and 0.772 (95% CI: 0.639-0.895). The model stratified patients into high‑ and low‑risk groups, with significantly different PFS between the two strata across all cohorts (log‑rank P < 0.05). Decision curve analysis supported the clinical utility of the integrated model.
Conclusions: A PET/CT‑based radiomic model integrating clinical, tumour, and whole‑body composition features provides robust, externally validated postoperative prognostic stratification for ESCC. This approach may facilitate individualised risk assessment and inform treatment decision‑making.
categories: Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging

paper.title: Enhanced Shallow-Feature Learning for Pediatric Renal Ultrasound Hydronephrosis Severity Classification.
paper.abstract:
Objective: Ultrasound severity grading of pediatric hydronephrosis guides whether a child receives surveillance, medical management or surgical referral, yet automated grading tools remain limited by single-vendor training, absence of external validation and unreported confidence reliability. This study develops and validates a four-class deep learning classifier (Healthy, Mild, Moderate, Severe) for pediatric renal ultrasound across multiple vendor systems, with external testing and confidence calibration analysis.
Methods: Tailored to speckle-dominated ultrasound, the classifier, HarDNetE3, extends harmonic dense connectivity with three modifications (shallow-to-deep skip connections, squeeze-and-excitation recalibration, residual stabilization) to preserve the boundary and texture cues most diagnostic of pelvic dilation. A multi-vendor archive of 222,523 images was curated through a reproducible pipeline combining ICD code filtering, OCR and LLM measurement validation, posterior view restriction and region-of-interest cropping, yielding 14,231 images from 5383 patients across three vendor systems.
Results: On the held-out test set, the classifier achieved an F1 score of 87.55% and a sensitivity of 87.63%, improving over the HarDNet85 baseline by +4.84 and +6.13 percentage points (p<0.001), respectively, and reduced high-confidence mis-classifications by 62.1%, relevant to safe triage, as such errors rarely prompt secondary review. Performance improved over the baseline on all three vendor data sets, although absolute performance varied considerably by vendor (macro F1 score 81.05%-98.34%). On a public external adult cohort differing in age, vendor and indication, the classifier achieved an F1 score of 92.54% without retraining in a binary, single-severity grade setting.
Conclusion: A multi-vendor, externally validated, calibration-aware classifier can grade pediatric hydronephrosis severity with clinically meaningful sensitivity and fewer high-confidence errors, supporting use as a decision-support tool alongside radiologist review. The underlying signal-informed design offers a transferable principle for other ultrasound classification tasks.

paper.title: Use of a large language model for identification and extraction of actionable details from recommendations for additional imaging in abdominopelvic CT reports.
paper.abstract:
Objective: Automated identification and extraction of recommendations for additional imaging (RAI) from radiology reports could facilitate closed-loop tracking and follow-up completion. We compare a prompt-engineered GPT-4.1 large language model (LLM) versus a validated encoder-only transformer deep learning model (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers [BERT]) for detection of RAI in abdominopelvic computed tomography (CTAP) reports, and evaluate GPT-4.1 for extraction of actionable RAI elements.
Methods: This retrospective study included CTAP reports from a multi-institution system in 2023. LLM and BERT were used to identify RAI from radiology reports; LLM also extracted RAI actionable elements (modality, body part, time frame, rationale). Recall, precision, F1, and accuracy for RAI detection were determined using human-annotated reference standard. Paired comparison between each model's accuracy used McNemar's test. LLM recall, precision, F1, and accuracy for actionable element extraction were computed. Element prevalence was compared using chi-square test.
Results: 2000 random reports for unique patients (58% women; mean age 58.5 ± 17.5) included 215 RAI within 206 reports. For RAI detection, GPT-4.1 recall, precision, F1 and accuracy were 95.6%, 98.5%, 97.0% and 99.4%, respectively; BERT recall, precision, F1 and accuracy were 93.7%, 96.5%, 95.1% and 99.0% (p = 0.16). Recommendation element recall were as follows: 100.0% for time frame, 93.9% for body part, 90.2% for rationale, and 94.2% for modality. Precision were 100.0%, 95.7%, 94.6% and 86.1%, respectively. 29/215 (13.5%) RAI were complete (specified all actionable elements). Prevalence of actionable elements varied (p < 0.001), highest for rationale (215/215, 100%), followed by body part (213/215, 99.1%), modality (191/215, 88.8%), and time frame (31/215, 14.4%).
Conclusion: GPT-4.1 demonstrated high accuracy for extraction of RAI and enabled accurate extraction of actionable elements. LLM integration into radiology workflows can facilitate automatic closed-loop communication and tracking of recommended imaging, which may reduce diagnostic delays.
